questions.stem: Which sequence correctly connects a protein-coding gene to phenotype?

options.text: DNA replication, transcription, gene duplication, phenotype
options.why: Replication copies DNA before cell division, and gene duplication isn't a normal stage of expression.

options.text: Transcription, translation, protein function, phenotype
options.why: The gene is transcribed into mRNA, the mRNA is translated, and the protein's function can affect phenotype.

options.text: Translation, transcription, protein folding, phenotype
options.why: The first two stages are backwards. DNA is transcribed before mRNA can be translated.

options.text: Transcription, DNA replication, protein function, phenotype
options.why: Replication isn't the step that converts an RNA message into a polypeptide. Translation belongs there.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes an enhancer from a transcription factor?

options.text: An enhancer is regulatory DNA, while a transcription factor is a protein that binds specific DNA
options.why: The enhancer supplies a binding sequence. An activator transcription factor can bind there and increase transcription.

options.text: An enhancer is a protein, while a transcription factor is the DNA sequence beside a gene
options.why: The molecule types have been reversed. Enhancers are DNA sequences, and transcription factors are proteins.

options.text: An enhancer produces mRNA, while a transcription factor translates that mRNA at a ribosome
options.why: RNA polymerase produces RNA, and ribosomes perform translation. Those aren't the roles of enhancers or transcription factors.

options.text: An enhancer copies a gene, while a transcription factor separates DNA strands before cell division
options.why: That describes neither component. Enhancers and transcription factors regulate transcription rather than DNA replication.

questions.stem: Two equally abundant mRNAs are translated at the same rate, but one remains intact much longer. What is the expected result?

options.text: The longer-lived mRNA produces more protein because it can undergo more rounds of translation
options.why: An mRNA that remains intact stays available to ribosomes for longer, allowing more protein molecules to be produced.

options.text: The shorter-lived mRNA produces more protein because nucleases release its amino acids more rapidly
options.why: Nucleases break RNA into nucleotides, not amino acids. Rapid degradation also reduces the time available for translation.

options.text: Both mRNAs produce equal protein because mRNA lifetime has no effect after transcription
options.why: Lifetime matters after transcription because an intact mRNA can be translated repeatedly before nucleases destroy it.

options.text: The longer-lived mRNA changes the DNA sequence because it remains paired with its gene
options.why: Mature mRNA doesn't stay paired with the gene or rewrite it. Stability changes translation, not the DNA sequence.

questions.stem: Why can a neuron and a muscle cell from one person have different proteomes?

options.text: Each cell type permanently removes genes that it no longer requires
options.why: Differentiation normally regulates genes rather than deleting them. Both cell types retain largely the same genome.

options.text: Each cell type expresses a different selection of genes from a largely shared genome
options.why: Different patterns of transcription and translation produce the proteins needed for each cell's specialized function.

options.text: Each cell type translates every gene but folds the resulting proteins differently
options.why: No cell expresses every gene. Much of the difference begins with selective transcription.

options.text: Each cell type receives a different genome when the zygote divides by mitosis
options.why: Mitosis normally passes equivalent genomes to daughter cells. Regulation of expression creates the different cell types.

questions.stem: Which description correctly compares a cell's transcriptome and proteome?

options.text: The transcriptome contains all DNA, while the proteome contains every possible amino acid
options.why: All DNA belongs to the genome. A proteome is a set of proteins, not a collection of free amino acids.

options.text: The transcriptome contains all RNA present at a time, while the proteome contains all proteins present or produced
options.why: Both reflect gene expression and can change with cell type, developmental stage and environmental conditions.

options.text: The transcriptome contains only mRNA, while the proteome contains only enzymes used in metabolism
options.why: A transcriptome includes other RNA types as well as mRNA, and a proteome includes structural and regulatory proteins as well as enzymes.

options.text: The transcriptome and proteome remain constant because the cell's genome remains constant
options.why: A stable genome can produce changing transcriptomes and proteomes when different genes are expressed.

questions.stem: What is the expected effect of methylating cytosine in the promoter of a gene?

options.text: Increased translation because the methyl groups attract additional ribosomes
options.why: Ribosomes translate mRNA and don't bind DNA promoters. The modification acts at transcription.

options.text: Repressed transcription and reduced expression of the downstream gene
options.why: Promoter DNA methylation represses transcription, so less of the gene's RNA and protein product is made.

options.text: Replacement of cytosine by a new base, producing a permanent mutation
options.why: The cytosine remains in the DNA sequence. A methyl tag modifies regulation without replacing the base.

options.text: Guaranteed activation of the gene because every methyl tag loosens chromatin
options.why: Promoter DNA methylation represses transcription. Histone methylation has more variable effects depending on its location.

questions.stem: Which statement about histone methylation is accurate?

options.text: It can activate or repress transcription depending on which histone amino acids are modified
options.why: Histone methylation doesn't have one universal effect. Its result depends on the modification site and cellular context.

options.text: It always represses transcription by changing the nucleotide sequence of nearby genes
options.why: Histone methylation leaves the DNA sequence unchanged and can be associated with activation or repression.

options.text: It increases translation by adding methylated amino acids to the growing polypeptide
options.why: The modification is added to histone proteins associated with DNA. It regulates transcription rather than building the translated polypeptide.

options.text: It removes nucleosomes from every active gene and exposes the entire chromosome
options.why: Histone methylation changes regulation at particular chromatin regions. It doesn't strip every nucleosome from a chromosome.

questions.stem: How can an epigenetic pattern be inherited by daughter cells after mitosis?

options.text: The nucleotide sequence changes before each division to encode the cell's current function
options.why: Stable differentiation doesn't require repeated mutation. The regulatory pattern can persist while the sequence stays unchanged.

options.text: DNA or histone tags are retained or copied, preserving a pattern of gene expression
options.why: Maintaining epigenetic tags helps daughter cells activate and repress the same genes as the parent cell.

options.text: Every mRNA molecule enters both daughter cells and remains intact for the organism's lifetime
options.why: mRNAs are eventually degraded, often within minutes or days. Long-term cellular memory depends on maintained regulation.

options.text: Only expressed genes are replicated, so inactive genes disappear from both daughter cells
options.why: The whole genome is replicated before mitosis. Expression status doesn't decide which DNA regions are copied.

questions.stem: Why are monozygotic twins useful for investigating environmental effects on gene expression?

options.text: They have nearly identical genomes, reducing genetic variation when differing exposures are compared
options.why: With much of the genetic difference controlled, differences in expression or epigenetic tags can be associated more strongly with environmental exposure.

options.text: They always experience identical prenatal conditions, so every later difference has one environmental cause
options.why: Prenatal environments can differ, and many later exposures can vary. A difference doesn't identify a single cause automatically.

options.text: They have identical epigenetic tags throughout life, allowing mutations to be measured directly
options.why: Their epigenetic patterns can diverge with development and exposure. Those differences are often what researchers investigate.

options.text: They have different genomes but share one environment, isolating the effects of DNA sequence
options.why: That reverses the comparison. Monozygotic twins have nearly identical genomes, while their environments may differ.

questions.stem: A liger and a tigon contain genetic material from lions and tigers but commonly differ in size. What best explains this observation?

options.text: Parent-of-origin epigenetic tags cause growth-related alleles to be expressed differently in the reciprocal crosses
options.why: Genomic imprinting makes expression depend on whether an allele came from the mother or father. This can produce different growth phenotypes.

options.text: The two crosses translate the genetic code differently because lions and tigers use different codons
options.why: Lions and tigers use the same genetic code. The difference concerns regulation of inherited alleles, not codon meaning.

options.text: A liger inherits only lion growth genes, whereas a tigon inherits only tiger growth genes
options.why: Both hybrids inherit genetic material from both species. What differs is which species supplied the maternal and paternal genomes.

options.text: The parental chromosomes blend after fertilization and create a new DNA base for each hybrid type
options.why: Parental alleles remain distinct, and genomic imprinting doesn't create new bases. Retained tags affect which alleles are expressed.

questions.stem: What happens when lactose becomes available to E. coli carrying the lac operon?

options.text: A lactose-derived inducer binds the repressor, preventing it from continuing to block the operator
options.why: Removing the repressor's block allows RNA polymerase to transcribe genes needed for lactose uptake and metabolism.

options.text: Lactose binds directly to the promoter and acts as the RNA polymerase that transcribes the genes
options.why: Lactose isn't a protein enzyme and doesn't transcribe DNA. It acts through the repressor protein.

options.text: The repressor binds more tightly to the operator, increasing transcription of the lactose-use genes
options.why: An operator-bound repressor blocks transcription. Lactose availability causes that repression to be removed.

options.text: The bacterium permanently mutates the operator so its descendants can digest lactose without regulation
options.why: The response is reversible regulation of transcription, not a permanent change in the operator's sequence.

questions.stem: How can estrogen alter gene expression in a target cell?

options.text: It crosses the membrane, binds an intracellular receptor, and the complex binds regulatory DNA
options.why: The hormone–receptor complex acts as a transcription factor and changes transcription of particular target genes.

options.text: It binds every cell's DNA directly and replaces bases in genes associated with reproduction
options.why: Estrogen acts through a receptor and doesn't replace DNA bases. Cells without the appropriate receptor won't respond in the same way.

options.text: It remains outside the cell and translates mRNA into estrogen-responsive proteins at the membrane
options.why: Ribosomes perform translation. Estrogen is lipid-soluble and can cross the membrane to bind an intracellular receptor.

options.text: It binds a nuclease and prevents degradation of every mRNA molecule produced by the cell
options.why: That would be broad control of mRNA stability. Estrogen regulates selected genes through its receptor and regulatory DNA.
